titre: A carbon-14 spike gave a year to the Viking camp in Newfoundland
accroche: For sixty years, the Viking site of L'Anse aux Meadows had only an approximate date. In 2021, three pieces of wood gave a felling year.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1960, the Norwegian Helge Ingstad follows a Newfoundland resident, George Decker, to a field of grassy mounds at L'Anse aux Meadows. The excavations that follow uncover eight buildings with turf walls, a large quantity of iron slag, and boat nails. Scandinavians lived there, nearly five centuries before Christopher Columbus.

One simple question remained: when? For sixty years, no one could answer to the exact year. The Icelandic sagas that mention voyages westward were not written down until several centuries after the events. And the 55 carbon-14 dates linked to the Norse occupation, mostly obtained in the 1960s and 1970s, are spread across the entire Viking Age: measurements of the time were less precise and required large samples, and the wood or charcoal dated may have grown well before it was used.

## A marker written in the rings

A carbon-14 date gives a range, not a year. To narrow it, the team of Margot Kuitems and Michael Dee, at the University of Groningen, relies on a cosmic accident. In 993, the atmosphere's carbon-14 content jumps by about 9 per mille under the effect of a cosmic-ray event. These jumps appear at the same time in trees across the planet.

In each ring, a tree fixes the carbon of the year in which it formed it. The 993 jump therefore leaves a mark in every tree alive at the time, whatever the continent. All that is needed is to find it in a piece of wood, then count the rings out to the bark: you obtain the year the tree was cut down.

## Three trees, one year

The researchers select three pieces of wood from Norse contexts at the site. All bear clean cuts made with a metal blade, which the indigenous peoples of the time did not make. They come from three different trees, of at least two species: two pieces of fir, perhaps balsam fir, and one of juniper or thuja, identification uncertain. In each case, the 993 jump is expected between 26 and 31 rings before the bark, and for each, the most probable fit gives the same felling year: 1021. The 95 percent interval runs from 1019 to 1024.

According to the authors, this is the only secure calendar date for a European presence on the other side of the Atlantic before Columbus's voyages.

## What the wood says, and what it does not

This date is that of a felling, not of a stay. The authors note that both the sagas and the remains are compatible with a very brief occupation; the felling year says nothing about its duration. The year is fixed; the length of the stay remains an open question.

repere.texte: For three pieces of wood cut with metal, from three different trees, the most probable fit places the felling year in 1021 CE.
repere.source: Kuitems et al., “Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021,” Nature, 601, 2021, pp. 388-391

carte.punch: A carbon-14 spike from the year 993 dated a Viking wood cutting in Newfoundland: 1021
carte.idee: Carbon-14 alone gives ranges. But in 993, a cosmic event marked the tree rings of the whole world. Three pieces of wood cut with metal at L'Anse aux Meadows all give 1021 as the most probable felling year.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Miyake, Masuda, and Nakamura, “Another rapid event in the carbon-14 content of tree rings,” Nature Communications, 2013
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English. The article that spotted the carbon-14 jump of 993 in tree rings.

quiz.question: Why does the carbon-14 jump of the year 993 make it possible to date a wood felling far more precisely than an isolated measurement?
choix: Because the Icelandic sagas give the year of each voyage, and the 993 jump serves only to confirm them
Because the carbon-14 measurement of a single ring is enough to read the year, with no outside marker or counting
Because it marks a ring carried by all trees then alive: counting out to the bark gives the felling year
Because the jump appears only in Newfoundland trees, which proves the wood is local and not imported
quiz.explication: The 993 jump is global, not specific to Newfoundland, and it is recorded in the rings: once the ring is found, all that remains is to count out to the bark. An isolated measurement gives only a range, and the sagas, written centuries later, do not date these voyages.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How is the L'Anse aux Meadows site discovered in 1960?
choix: The Norwegian Helge Ingstad spots it from the air during an exploration flight
Helge Ingstad is led to it by George Decker, a Newfoundland resident
Canadian archaeologists discover it while digging a road
Local fishermen report ruins after a storm
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1960, the Norwegian Helge Ingstad follows George Decker, a Newfoundland resident, to the field of grassy mounds where the excavations would uncover the Norse buildings.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the felling year of 1021 say about the length of the Viking stay at L'Anse aux Meadows?
choix: It proves that the occupation lasted at least one full generation
It proves that the site was occupied continuously until the 12th century
It says nothing about the length of the stay, which remains an open question
It shows that the Vikings left the same year, right after the wood was cut
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The felling year dates a cutting, not a stay: the authors note that sagas and remains are compatible with a very brief occupation, and the exact length remains an open question.
